evidence: backend/servers/api-server/src/client_ip.rs:236-252 — resolve_client_ip trusts CF-Connecting-IP whenever the socket peer is in the trusted set, but the default trusted set (private_defaults at client_ip.rs:167-173: loopback + RFC1918/RFC4193) is the exact nginx/container-ingress deployment the module docs call the common case. A plain reverse proxy does NOT strip an inbound CF-Connecting-IP header, so any client can send `CF-Connecting-IP: <forged>`; the peer (nginx, private range) is trusted, so the forged value is returned as the client IP — reintroducing the #2789 spoof (audit-log poisoning + per-request throttle-bucket rotation) that the rightmost-untrusted-XFF logic (client_ip.rs:212-223) otherwise closes.

cf_connecting_ip (client_ip.rs:199-201) is preferred over XFF with no left/right disambiguation and no Cloudflare-specific gate: the header is consulted purely on socket-peer trust, not on any assertion that the trusted edge is actually Cloudflare.

Fix: only consult CF-Connecting-IP when the trusted edge is explicitly Cloudflare — gate it behind a dedicated flag / CF-ranges config, not on the generic private-range default set. When the edge is a generic reverse proxy, fall through to the existing rightmost-untrusted-XFF resolution. Add a unit test asserting that a forged CF-Connecting-IP from a private-range peer with no Cloudflare gate is NOT returned as the client IP. Landable as a self-contained change to resolve_client_ip + config plumbing + a test; no schema/migration, no mobile dependency.

Confidence medium: the trust-on-peer path and the private-range default set are confirmed by static read; 'medium' rather than 'high' because whether a live deployment is exploitable depends on whether the operator's real ingress is Cloudflare (safe) or a generic private-range reverse proxy (exploitable), a deployment fact not verifiable in this static Rust-only pass.

backend/servers/api-server/src/services/workflow_executor.rs:611-652 — the workflow condition comparators are inconsistent about JSON type coercion. Eq (:612 `Ok(field_value == *compare_value)`), Ne (:613), In (:639-645 `arr.contains(&field_value)`) and NotIn (:646-652) use serde_json::Value's STRICT structural equality, where `json!(100) != json!("100")` and `json!(true) != json!("true")` — no string<->number/bool coercion.

But the ordering comparators on the SAME field DO coerce: Gt/Gte/Lt/Lte (:614-617) route through compare_numeric -> coerce_finite_f64 (:727-731), which parses numeric strings, and Contains/StartsWith/EndsWith (:618-638) stringify both sides via to_string()/as_str(). So `amount >= 100` matches whether the trigger field or the stored condition value is the number 100 or the string "100", while `amount == 100` matches ONLY when both sides are the exact same JSON type.

Impact: workflow conditions are authored in a UI form and stored as JSON in workflow.conditions; form inputs commonly serialize scalar values as STRINGS (e.g. condition value "3", "true", "100"), whereas trigger_event fields (get_field_value at :671-694, traverse_json :697-715) carry the natively-typed JSON emitted by the event producer (a numeric amount/priority/count is a JSON number). An equality guard such as priority == 3 (stored value "3") then NEVER matches the numeric trigger field, so an Eq-guarded automation silently never fires; symmetrically a Ne / NotIn guard is always-true and lets actions run unguarded. A `>=`/`contains` guard on the very same field behaves correctly, which makes the failure look non-deterministic to an operator and hard to diagnose.

Distinct from the prior workflow findings: code-review-api-core-workflow-notin-fail-open covered NotIn returning true when compare_value is NOT an array (a different branch — the `else` arm at :649-651); this finding is about the strict-vs-coercing TYPE mismatch inside the happy path of Eq/Ne/In/NotIn. Both can bite the same condition.

Fix: make Eq/Ne/In/NotIn coerce consistently with the ordering/string operators — e.g. attempt numeric equality via coerce_finite_f64 first (so 100 == "100"), fall back to case-consistent string comparison, and for In/NotIn apply the same element-wise coercion — OR normalize condition values to their typed JSON at store time and document that conditions are type-strict. Add a unit test asserting `{field: "trigger.amount" (number 100), op: Eq, value: "100"}` evaluates true (fails on current code). Landable as a self-contained change to evaluate_single_condition + a test; no schema/migration, no mobile dependency.

Confidence medium: the operator asymmetry, the strict serde_json::Value equality, and the coercing compare_numeric/to_string paths are all confirmed by static read; 'medium' rather than 'high' because whether a live workflow trips it depends on how the condition-builder UI serializes scalar values (string vs typed), which is a frontend-side fact not verified in this static Rust-only pass.

backend/servers/api-server/src/services/document_generation.rs:496-502 — in summarize_document's very-long-document branch, request.content (a String) is sliced by BYTE offset with no UTF-8 char-boundary check: `let half_limit = char_limit / 2;` then `let start = &request.content[..half_limit.min(request.content.len())];`, `let end_start = request.content.len().saturating_sub(half_limit);`, `let end = &request.content[end_start..];`. Indexing a str/String by a byte range that does not fall on a char boundary PANICS ('byte index N is not a char boundary').

The `.min(len())` / saturating_sub only guard the RANGE bounds (out-of-range), not char-boundary ALIGNMENT. half_limit is char_limit/2 = (max_context*4)/2 = 200_000 bytes; byte offsets 200_000 (from the front) and len-200_000 (from the back) are arbitrary positions that in practice land mid-character.

This product is Slovak/Czech/German-first (i18n sk, cs, de, en per the repo architecture). Real lease agreements, contracts, and long documents fed to summarize_document are full of multi-byte UTF-8 (á č ď é í ľ ň ó š ť ž ä ö ü ß …). Any document large enough to enter this branch (content_tokens > max_context = 100_000 tokens, ~400_000 chars at the code's own ~4-chars/token estimate) that contains a multi-byte char adjacent to either 200_000-byte cut point panics — which for non-ASCII long documents is the common case, not an edge case.

Reachability/severity: this is on a user-facing feature (document summarization) reachable from an api-server request handler. Axum isolates a handler-task panic into a 500 for that one request rather than crashing the process, so it is not a server-wide DoS — but the specific document can NEVER be summarized (every retry re-panics), and it surfaces as an opaque 500 with a panic in the logs rather than a handled error. Bounded blast radius = request-scoped, hence score_delta 2 (not 3).

Distinct from the prior document_generation findings code-review-api-core-docgen-empty-llm-ok / docgen-empty-llm-blank-doc, which both concern the `unwrap_or_default()` collapse of a missing LLM completion at :536-540 — a different location and defect class from this input-side slicing panic at :496-502.

Fix: cut on char boundaries instead of raw byte offsets — e.g. use `str::char_indices()` / `floor_char_boundary` (or take/rev-take over `.chars()`) to pick the nearest boundary <= half_limit, or operate on `char` counts (`content.chars().take(n)` for the head and a matching tail). Add a regression test that summarizes a >400k-char string containing multi-byte chars straddling both cut points and asserts no panic. Self-contained Rust change + test; no mobile/AGP dependency.

Confidence medium: the byte-offset String slicing and the absence of any char-boundary alignment are confirmed by static read; 'medium' rather than 'high' only because triggering requires an input that both exceeds the ~400k-char truncation threshold AND has a multi-byte char at a cut point — realistic for this locale but not confirmed at runtime in this static-only pass.

Many list endpoints resolve the client-supplied page size as `query.limit.unwrap_or(N)` with NO upper-bound clamp, then pass that value straight into the repository as the SQL `LIMIT`. A client can therefore send `?limit=100000000` and force the database to plan/materialize an unbounded result set — a cheap unauthenticated-shaped resource-exhaustion / DoS on any org member's endpoint. Unclamped sites include ai/sessions.rs:101 (unwrap_or 50), :205 (unwrap_or 100), :924, :997; ai/equipment.rs:203/:297/:379; ai/voice.rs:317; ai/workflows.rs:546 (`query.limit.unwrap_or(50) as usize` — the cast also silently wraps a hostile i64); ai/llm.rs:1448; vendors/contacts.rs:130; compliance.rs:167/:240/:268 (unwrap_or 100); predictive_maintenance.rs:316/:503/:536.

CONFIRMED end-to-end for the ai_chat path: routes/ai/sessions.rs:205 passes `query.limit.unwrap_or(100)` into `ai_chat_repo.list_session_messages(..., limit, offset)`, and crates/db/src/repositories/ai_chat.rs:229-247 binds that `limit: i64` directly into `... LIMIT $4 OFFSET $5` (`.bind(limit)` at line 247) with no `.min()`/`clamp` anywhere in the repo. So the user value reaches Postgres LIMIT unmodified. The same repo file repeats the pattern at :137/:156/:160 and :365/:377/:381.

The intended pattern already exists in the hardened admin handlers, which makes the omission a clear inconsistency rather than a debatable design choice: admin/users.rs:58 `q.limit.unwrap_or(20).min(100)` and admin/audit.rs:261 `q.limit.unwrap_or(100).min(500)` / :280 `.unwrap_or(10_000).min(50_000)` all clamp. market_pricing.rs:1665 `.unwrap_or(10).min(50)` clamps too. The list endpoints above simply never got the `.min(cap)`.

Fix: clamp every user-supplied limit at the handler boundary with a per-endpoint `.min(MAX_PAGE_SIZE)` (or a shared `Pagination::clamped()` helper), mirroring the admin handlers; belt-and-suspenders, add a defensive clamp in the repository methods that take a raw `limit: i64`. Landable as a single backend-only PR (routes + ai_chat repo), no mobile/AGP dependency. IG3: a handler/integration test asserting `?limit=1000000` returns at most MAX rows fails on any branch missing the clamp.

Confidence medium: the unclamped flow to SQL LIMIT is statically confirmed for the ai_chat path (route -> repo -> `.bind(limit)`), and the missing `.min()` is visible at each listed call site; 'medium' not 'high' because a subset of the listed endpoints route through repos that could re-clamp internally (not individually traced for all 18 sites) and because the practical blast radius depends on row width and DB timeouts.

routes/ai/ocr.rs:197-208 — when the image bytes are present but `state.storage_service` is None (storage unavailable), the handler does not fail or defer; it persists the meter reading with a FABRICATED `photo_url = format!("pending-upload/{}/{}", meter_id, Uuid::new_v4())` (line 207) that points at no stored object, then returns `StatusCode::CREATED` (line 228) as if the photo-backed reading succeeded.

Landable as a small backend-only change in ai/ocr.rs (+ optionally a pending-upload table/migration). IG3: a handler test with storage disabled asserts the endpoint does NOT return 201 with a `pending-upload/` photo_url.

Confidence medium: the fabricated-URL-under-201 flow is confirmed by direct read of ai/ocr.rs:197-239; 'medium' because whether storage_service is ever actually None in the deployed config (vs always wired) is environment-dependent, so the severity is 'latent under degraded storage' rather than always-on.

frontend/apps/mobile/src/qrcode/DeepLinkHandler.ts:215-217 — DeepLinkManager.initialize() calls `Linking.addEventListener('url', (event) => this.handleUrl(event.url))` but discards the returned subscription. On React Native 0.85 (this repo's version) addEventListener returns an EmitterSubscription that must be removed via `subscription.remove()`; the class captures nothing and exposes no teardown/dispose method (grep for remove/teardown/dispose/subscription in the file returns none), so the runtime 'url' listener leaks for the process lifetime.

The listener is also non-idempotent across re-initialisation: any second call to initialize() registers a SECOND 'url' listener while the first is never removed, so every runtime deep link then invokes handleUrl -> dispatchLink N times (N = number of initialize() calls), double-firing the registered handler and causing duplicate navigation/side-effects per link.

frontend/apps/mobile/src/hooks/useDeepLinkRouting.ts:36-48 — the wiring effect returns `unsubscribe` (from deepLinkManager.addHandler) as its cleanup, which removes only the HANDLER, not the Linking 'url' listener created inside initialize(). So on unmount the Linking listener is orphaned, and on remount initialize() runs again and stacks another one. The hook's own JSDoc asserts it 'avoids duplicate handlers / re-initialisation' — true for the handler and for onNavigate-identity churn (fixed via onNavigateRef + [] deps), but NOT for the Linking subscription, which has no teardown counterpart. React Fast Refresh re-runs the effect in dev (guaranteed duplication there); a production remount of the hook's host (e.g. an auth-driven navigator swap) would do the same.

Distinct from the dropped item code-review-mobile-rn-deeplink-init-unhandled (that flagged initialize() re-running on onNavigate identity + a `void ... ` with no .catch — both since remediated in current code via the ref pattern and an explicit `.catch` at useDeepLinkRouting.ts:44). This finding is the uncaptured Linking subscription / missing DeepLinkManager teardown, which no filed item covers.

Fix: capture the subscription in initialize() (e.g. `this.urlSub = Linking.addEventListener('url', ...)`), guard against double-init (return early or remove the prior sub if already initialised), add a `teardown()`/`dispose()` that calls `this.urlSub?.remove()`, and have useDeepLinkRouting's effect cleanup call it alongside `unsubscribe`. Severity low: deepLinkManager is a singleton typically mounted once at the app root, so prod impact is a single leaked listener rather than unbounded duplication — but the leak is real and the duplicate-dispatch is a live hazard under Fast Refresh and any host remount. Confidence medium: the missing capture/teardown is confirmed by static read; the duplication's production reachability depends on the hook-host lifecycle (traced, not runtime-confirmed).
